summary: Proposes a fragment-oriented solution for the real-time encapsulation part of an architecture for combining multi-link PPP with multiple classes of traffic.

eli5.summary: A way to chop big messages into pieces so urgent small ones can slip between.

questions: how does ppp multilink support real-time traffic
what is prefix elision in ppp
how many priority classes does multi-class ppp support
subtitle: Spare bits in the PPP Multilink header become a class number, so urgent real-time fragments can slip between pieces of big packets on slow links.

tldr.problem: On a slow modem link, one 1500 byte packet blocks real-time traffic for about 400 ms, which is unacceptable for real-time conversation.
tldr.mechanism: The PPP Multilink fragment header gets a class number, and each class runs its own copy of Multilink with a separate sequence number space and reassembly buffer. Two new LCP options negotiate the format and an optional prefix that is dropped from each packet.
tldr.outcome: Short packets can be sent between fragments of longer ones at several priority levels. It is a Proposed Standard and the text says its security is no better and no worse than PPP Multilink.

today: RFC 2686 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Fragment for Real-Time Traffic
sections.content:
RFC 2686 defines the fragment-oriented real-time encapsulation format for an architecture that carries integrated services over low-bitrate links, described in RFC 2689. It starts from the PPP Multilink protocol (RFC 1990) and adds a small number of extensions to add functionality and reduce overhead.

The motivation is delay. A 1500 byte packet on a 28.8 kbit/s modem link makes the link unavailable for real-time information for about 400 ms. That pushes real-time applications to round-trip delays of at least a second. The extensions let a sender split packets of various priorities into classes of fragments, so high-priority packets go out between fragments of lower priorities.

A companion document (RFC 2687) defines a suspend/resume-oriented solution for cases where the best possible delay is required.
sections.eli5: A big message on a slow line makes everyone else wait. Cutting it into pieces lets urgent little messages go first.

sections.title: Requirements for the Scheme
sections.content:
The main goal is to minimise end-to-end delay, in particular the worst-case delay, since that sets the playout points applications choose. Overhead must be kept small, and non-real-time flows should still get the usual MTU.

The RFC estimates that the largest packet is the default MTU of 1500 bytes and the smallest high-priority packets are about 22 bytes (compressed RTP/G.723.1), which suggests a maximum need of about eight levels of suspension. On 28.8kbit/s modems at least two levels seem practically required.

Further requirements: predictable behaviour for admission control, robustness against errors at least at PPP's level of error detection, cooperation with PPP (with an unambiguous fall back to standard LCP), compatibility with existing HDLC-based chips and routers, and being future proof, for example as V.80 based modems emerge.
sections.eli5: The goal is that urgent messages wait as little as possible, the extra labels stay small, and normal big messages still fit.

sections.title: Using PPP Multilink As-Is
sections.content:
PPP Multilink (MP) already splits packets into fragments using sequence numbers and begin/end bits. A fragment carries a PPP header, an MP header with the B and E bits and a sequence number, the fragment data and the FCS.

Used as is, MP supports two levels of priority: big packets sent through multilink can be suspended by small packets sent outside multilink without a multilink header. But the single monotonically increasing sequence number means the fragments of one packet cannot be interrupted to send another multilink packet, so there is only one level of suspension. Packets sent outside multilink are not fragmentable.

The RFC also notes that the multilink header is relatively large, which is a problem this document does not solve when delay bounds become small.
sections.eli5: The old system can only let tiny messages cut in front of one kind of big message, and its labels are a little bulky.

sections.title: Classes in the Multilink Header
sections.content:
The obvious fix is to run Multilink several times over one link. Multilink allows only one instance, but some header bits are unused: two in the short sequence number format and six in the long format. This document uses some of them as a class number.

Each class runs a separate copy of the mechanism in RFC 1990, with its own sequence number space and reassembly buffer. In the short format the header holds B, E, a 2-bit class (cls) and the sequence number. In the long format it holds B, E, a 4-bit class, two zero bits and the sequence number.

Together with the ability to send packets without a multilink header, this gives four levels of suspension with 12-bit headers and sixteen levels with 24-bit headers. Only four of the six free bits are used in the long format.
sections.eli5: Each kind of message gets its own numbered lane, so the pieces of a big message in one lane do not block the other lanes.

sections.title: Negotiated Options and Prefix Elision
sections.content:
Two new PPP LCP options are defined. The Multilink Header Format option (Type 27, Length 4) carries a code and a number of suspendable classes. Code 2 means the long sequence number format with classes and code 6 means the short format with classes. The number of suspendable classes bounds the allowed class numbers. Implementations SHOULD at least support 4 for the short format and 8 for the long format.

When the option is negotiated, the accepting side MUST either send all later multilink packets in that format or Configure-Nak or Configure-Reject it. If only an MRRU option is present, long headers with class 0 only are used by default.

The Prefix Elision option (Type 26) maps a class to a prefix of bytes, such as a common protocol identifier, that is removed from each packet before sending and implicitly added back after reassembly. It is not a replacement for header or data compression. A receiver willing to accept prefix-elided packets SHOULD request the option with empty content, and the sender can then propose the mapping with Configure-Nak.
sections.eli5: Two sides agree beforehand how many lanes there are, and may agree to skip words that every message in a lane starts with.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC gives a single sentence: operation of the protocol is believed to be no more and no less secure than operation of the PPP multilink protocol. It adds no new security mechanisms.
sections.eli5: It is about as safe as the system it builds on, no better and no worse.
